=== Morphological Assessment Form ===
A. Leaf Arrangement & Architecture
    1. Leaf relative position (alternate / opposite / whorled): alternate (leaves are attached at successive nodes along the stem, alternating sides; no paired or whorled arrangement visible)
    2. Leaf spacing (clustered / distal): clustered (leaves appear grouped near the apex of the stem, with no long internodes between leaf nodes)
B. Leaf Complexity
    3. Leaf complexity (simple / compound): compound (each leaf is composed of multiple leaflets attached to a central rachis)
    4. Compound leaf type, ONLY if leaf complexity is compound (odd-pinnate / even-pinnate): odd-pinnate (the terminal leaflet is present, with leaflets arranged in pairs along the rachis)
    5. Number of leaflets (integer estimate 2, 4, 8, …): 8 (each compound leaf has 4 leaflets on each side of the rachis plus a terminal leaflet, totaling 9; however, some leaves appear to have 3–4 leaflets per side, so 8 is the most consistent estimate across visible leaves)
    6. Leaflet arrangement (opposite / alternate / subopposite): alternate (leaflets are arranged alternately along the rachis, not in direct pairs)
C. Leaf Morphology
    7. Leaf margin (entire / toothed) AND if toothed (dentate, serrate, etc.)): entire (margins are smooth with no visible teeth or serrations)
    8. Leaf shape (elliptic, obovate, lanceolate, etc.): elliptic (leaflets are broadly oval with rounded base and tapering apex)
    9. Leaf apex (acute, obtuse, acuminate): acute (leaflets taper to a sharp point at the tip)
    10. Leaf base (rounded, cordate, cuneate): rounded (base of leaflets is broadly rounded, not tapered or heart-shaped)
    11. Venation type (pinnate / palmate / parallel): pinnate (main vein runs from base to apex, with secondary veins branching off laterally)
    12. Secondary veins (visibility, spacing, number): visible, moderately spaced, 3–5 pairs per leaflet (secondary veins are clearly visible and run from midrib to margin, with moderate spacing)
    13. Leaf surface features (glabrous, shiny, dull, rugose): glabrous, dull (surface appears smooth without hairs, with a matte finish; not glossy)
    14. Leaf surface trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs or trichomes on leaf surface)
    15. Petiole length (short / long): short (petioles are relatively short, supporting the compound leaf structure without elongation)
    16. Petiole features (winged / grooved / terete): terete (petioles are round in cross-section, without wings or grooves)
D. Stem & Shoot Traits
    17. Stem type, may not be visible (woody / herbaceous): herbaceous (stem appears green, soft, and flexible, typical of young seedlings; no visible bark or woody texture)
    18. Stem trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs on stem surface)
    19. Stem color: green (stem is uniformly green, with slight reddish tinge at base in some images)
    20. Stem texture (smooth / ridged / lenticellate): smooth (surface is even and unbroken, without ridges or lenticels)
E. Other Visible Seedling Traits
    21. Stipules, sometimes visible only in close-up images (present / absent): absent (no stipules observed at leaf bases)
    22. Latex, rarely visible but extremely diagnostic when present (present / not observed): not observed (no exudate visible when stem or leaf is broken; no latex seen)
    23. Pulvinus, for Fabaceae family only (present / absent): absent (no swollen joints at leaflet bases visible; pulvinus not observed)
    24. Tendrils (present / absent): absent (no tendrils observed on stem or leaf structures)

Locating an individual
It is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Distribution
From Belize to Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is widely distributed in the medium to low elevations of both slopes, in climates ranging from humid to very humid, although it prefers climates with marked seasonality; 0-700-800 m.
Habit
Trees, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown outer bark.
Bark
Outer bark reddish-brown, scaly, inner bark reddish with a pleasant mango scent; white or milky resinous sap.
Leaves
Odd-pinnate leaves, with 7-9 leaflets, elliptical, oblong, or oblong-lanceolate, 5-21 x 4-7.2 cm, apex acuminate to abruptly acuminate, base obtuse to asymmetric, generally glabrous; petiolules without evident pulvini, margin entire; petioles 4-14 cm long.
Flowers
Inflorescences are panicles, 3-15 cm long, axillary. Yellowish or greenish-yellow flowers (unisexual); calyx with 5 lobes, 1-1.5 mm long, cuculiform; petals (tubular corolla), with 5 lobes, 5-5.5 mm long; stamens 10, 1 mm long, filaments inserted at the base of the disc; annular disc with 10 lobes; ovary with 5 lobes, ovoid, with 5 locules; style 1, stigma with 5 lobes.
Fruits
Capsular and drupe-like fruits, 1.5-2.5 x 1.5 x 3 cm, ovoid or more or less turbinate, with 2-5 lobes, dehiscent by 4-5 valves, scarlet red inside, red to black when mature; pyrenes 3-5, 12-13 mm thick, white, the mesocarp (pseudoaril) reddish turning white upon exposure (dehiscence), fleshy, juicy, sweet, and edible.
Diagnosis
Characterized by being a large tree, the bark on mature trees is somewhat scaly, lenticellate, and the inner bark has a very particular and pleasant mango scent. At the vegetative level, it is sometimes confused with the genus Protium, although its leaves lack pulvinated petiolules and the turpentine aroma when crushed. Its fruits are distinctive for their peculiar turbinate shape.
Habitat
In the Forest; it is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Phenology
Flowers observed in June and August; fruits in August and February.

Guavita cansa-boca, Bribri, Guava, Guava del mono Tree, to 15 m tall; branchlets sparsely strigose when young, glabrate in age, minutely lenticellate, minutely ribbed below petioles (at least when dried). Leaves strigose throughout, especially on axis and midrib of leaflets; petiole and rachis terete to narrowly margined; leaflets in 2 or 3 pairs, lanceolate to elliptic, long-acuminate, acute to rounded at base, the terminal pair 9-18 cm long, 3.5-7.5 cm wide. Spikes axillary, in groups of 1-7; peduncle and rachis strigose; peduncles 2-4 cm long; rachis much shorter, 1-2.5 cm long; bracts subulate, to ± 2 mm long; calyx puberulent, 3-5 mm long, the lobes ± 1 mm long; corolla moderately sericeous, 5-9 mm long, the lobes to 2 mm long; stamens and style to ca 2 cm long. Legumes flat, to 16 cm long and 2 cm wide, minutely puberulent, the margins raised.

Tree, 5-20 m tall; outer bark minutely fissured, thin (bearing short, raised, horizontal lines on inner surface); inner bark reddish-brown on the outer edge, bearing impressed short horizontal lines, the sap with sweet, distinctive aroma; young twigs, rachises, axes of inflorescences and of leaves moderately short-appressed pubescent, glabrous in age. Leaves alternate, pinnate, mostly 8-25 cm long, essentially glabrous; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets usually alternate, often dimorphic, those of full size usually 3-5, often with 1 or 2 pairs of minute, aborted leaflets at base, rarely with 7 full-sized leaflets, the blades ± elliptic, acuminate, acute to obtuse at base, 6-16 cm long, 2.5-6(7) cm wide; major lateral veins mostly 8-12, scarcely raised below, joining before the margin, the midrib usually flat above. Panicles solitary in upper axils, 5-17 cm long; flowers greenish, mostly 5-parted; calyx bowl-shaped, shallowly lobed, 1-2 mm long, glabrate; petals ovate, 2-3 mm long, usually glabrous but with minute papillae on margin; staminal tube one-half to two-thirds as long as petals, much broader than long, moderately to sparsely pubescent outside at least toward base (often glabrous outside in South America), sparsely to densely pubescent inside; anthers twice the number of petals, slender, slightly tapered toward apex, ca 1 mm long, dehiscing along lateral margins, alternating with and ± equaling acicular lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, 1-2 mm wide, with 2 or 3 (4) locules, the trichomes dense, appressed, white on basal half; style ± equaling ovary at anthesis; stigma capitate, inconspicuously lobed, held about at height of anthers. Fruits ± globose, green at maturity, weakly verrucose, 2-3 cm diam, ± glabrous, dehiscing by 3 valves; seeds 1 or 2, covered with a shiny red aril. Rare; collected only along the shore between Bat Cove and the dock. Flowers from March to May. The fruits mature from August to September.

Tree, to 30 m tall and 40 cm dbh (often much shorter along the shore); outer bark hard, closely fissured; inner bark red; younger stems, leaf rachises, and axes of inflorescences densely strigose and puberulent (in Panama) or sparsely strigose, sparsely puberulent, or nearly glabrous (often in South America). Leaves alternate, imparipinnate, mostly 15-30 cm long; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets apparently never dimorphic, usually 5-9 (rarely 3 or 10), usually alternate, ± elliptic, acuminate, obtuse-attenuate at base, 4-21 cm long, 1.5-8 cm wide, usually glabrous or minutely puberulent and/or strigose on midrib on both surfaces, rarely strigose below; midrib sharply raised. Panicles axillary (often appearing terminal), mostly 8-20 cm long; flowers white or greenish-yellow, 4-6-parted, as wide as long, globular in bud, the trichomes (at least on calyx) erect or appressed; calyx saucer-shaped, the lobes acute or blunt; petals valvate, ovate, to ca 2 mm long, glabrous or sparsely appressed-pubescent outside, glabrous inside, the margins papillose-puberulent; staminal tube two-thirds to three-fourths as long as petals, broader than long, glabrous outside and in but sometimes pubescent inside near apex, the lobes narrowly acute; anthers twice as many as petals, very narrowly ovoid, ca 0.5 mm long, alternating with and usually longer than lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, densely appressed-pubescent with white trichomes all over; style usually glabrous. Capsules ellipsoid, 11-18 mm long, orange at maturity, prominently tuberculate, the 3 (4) valves folding back to expose shiny red aril; seeds 1 or 2, smooth, ellipsoid, ca 1 cm long. Abundant as seedlings; common as adults in the forest, especially in the old forest. Flowering is bimodal, but principally from April to June, especially in June; a second but much smaller flowering period may occur from September to November. [unclear reference] The fruits from the first flowering mature mostly during September and October, especially in October; mature fruits from the second flowering have been seen in June.

Functionally unisexual tree, to 18 m tall, to 27 cm dbh; outer bark thin, flaking in firm sheets, lenticellate; inner bark moderately thick, reddish; sap slowly forming viscid, cloudy droplets after slash, with strong, sweet aroma; stems glabrous, prominently brown-lenticellate. Leaves imparipinnate; petioles flattened above with sharp margins; petiolules thickened at both ends; leaflets 5-9 (13), mostly oblong to oblong-elliptic, acuminate with blunt acumen, acute to rounded at base, often ± inequilateral, 10-20(27) cm long, 5-9(12) cm wide, glabrous except for minute papillae. Panicles axillary, near stem apex, the branches ferruginous; staminate inflorescences somewhat larger than pistillate inflorescences (to 24 cm long); flowers 5-parted, sessile, 3.5-5 mm long; calyx to 2 mm long, cupulate, 5-lobed, minutely pubescent, the lobes acute; petals lanceolate, yellow-green, thickened medially on outside, ca 3 mm long, erect to somewhat spreading at anthesis; stamens 10, alternately long and short, the longest to 2 mm long, the shortest to 1.3 mm long, scarcely longer than the prominent, pubescent disk; ovary ovoid, densely pubescent; style short, the ovary and style together ca 2.7 mm long; stigma 5-lobed, persisting in fruit. Capsules drupaceous, bearing 1-5 pyrenes, ovoid to depressed-globose, with 4 or 5 lobes (rarely 2- or 3-lobed), mostly 2-3 cm diam, red at maturity, usually rounded at both ends, the carpels 4 or 5, each dehiscing by a single valve, the valve falling free to expose the white mesocarp surrounding the pyrene; pyrenes black, 1 per carpel, 1-seeded, ovoid in face view, irregular in side view. Croat 11109, 14822. Common along the shore; occasional in the forest. Flowers chiefly in April and May. The fruits mature chiefly in the middle of the rainy season (August to October). Small bees, possibly Trigona species, have been seen visiting the flowers. The fruits are edible. Costa Rica and Panama. In Panama, known only from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Chiriqui Province, Panama, and Darien Province. Reported from tropical wet forest in Costa Rica (Holdridge et al, 1971).

Dioecious shrub or tree, to 15 m tall; trunk slender or to 20 cm dbh and deeply invaginated; stems sericeous when very young, glabrate in age, with conspicuous leaf scars. Leaves somewhat clustered at apex of branchlets; stipules caducous, to 1 cm long, sericeous, leaving a conspicuous interpetiolar line of trichomes; petioles 6-14 mm long, sericeous to glabrate; blades ovate-elliptic to obovate-elliptic, abruptly short-acuminate, usually obtuse and ± decurrent onto petiole at base, 7-13(21) cm long, 3.5-8 (12) cm wide, glabrous or with sparse long trichomes on major veins below and tufts of trichomes in axils, the margins ciliate and ± revolute.

Locating an individual
Central Road (CC) 1300 m, Left.
Distribution
From Honduras to Bolivia, Paraguay, and southeastern Brazil. In Costa Rica, widespread in mainly very humid climates on both slopes, 10-1,300 m.
Habit
Tree, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown bark, slightly scaly, inner color pink and with slight resinous-milky secretion, short branches; glabrous twigs; stipules absent.
Bark
Reddish-brown bark, slightly scaly, inner color pink and with slight resinous-milky secretion.
Leaves
Compound odd-pinnate leaves, alternate, leaflets 5-13, 7.5-23 x 2.5-11.2 cm, elliptical to oblong-elliptical, apex short-acuminate, base asymmetric, opposite, glabrous or slightly pubescent on the underside near the central vein, margin entire; petiole 4-20 cm long.
Flowers
Flowers (unisexual) white to yellowish-green and cream; sepals 5, 0.4-0.9 mm long; petals 5, 1.4-2.2 mm long; stamens (8-) 10, unequal, staminodes present in pistillate flowers. The inflorescences have a broad subterminal panicle, with many flowers, 10-35 cm long, rusty-puberulent.
Fruits
Fruit a drupe, 1-1.8 x 0.8-1.3 cm, ovoid, oblong or obovoid, exocarp dark purple to black, endocarp cartilaginous.
Seeds
Seed 1.
Diagnosis
Characterized by its compound leaves, leaflets with entire margins, asymmetric at the base and secondary veins weakly forming a submarginal vein (brochidodromous venation), young leaves with silky pubescence on the underside. Its vegetative appearance and trunk color, as well as its inner bark, resemble or may confuse it with a species of Trichilia (Meliaceae), hence its vernacular names. In mature trees, when making a cut on the trunk, it secretes a slight milky sap in the cambium area.
Habitat
In the rainforest, both in primary forest and secondary vegetation.
Phenology
Flowers observed in May, fruits in October.

Adult plants frequent in the forest; seedlings common and recognizable by the large orbicular fimbriate stipules. Flowers in the late rainy season (August to November). The fruits mature within 1 month. Costa Rica to Peru and Brazil. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone and Colon and from premontane wet forest in the Canal Zone (Pipeline Road), Veraguas, and Panama (Cerro Jefe). [Paullinia turbacensis] is a tendriled liana; stems terete, ± glabrous, bearing conspicuous brown lenticels; sap at periphery milky, not copious. Leaves trifoliolate; petioles to 14 cm long, with marginal ribs above, glabrate; leaflets broadly elliptic, acuminate or acute at apex, attenuate to rounded at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-12 cm wide (to 23 cm long and 11 cm wide as juveniles), glabrate but with axillary tufts below, subentire to remotely crenate-dentate. Thyrses small, helicoid, to 7 cm long, solitary or clustered at nodes, often on leafless stems near the ground but occurring to 5 m high; flowers white, ca 5 mm long; petals with the scales ca two-thirds as long as petals, yellow-crested, the anterior scales bilobed, their appendages pubescent, the glands white, acute, densely pubescent; staminal cluster equaling petals; filaments densely pubescent; nectar abundant, stored near the large glands; ovary glabrous; styles pubescent. Capsules elliptic to obovate, 2 cm long, red, short-pubescent, the 3 boat-shaped valves broadly spreading to expose seeds; seeds 1-3, black, shiny, less than 1 cm long, covered on the lower half by a fleshy white aril, dangling on a thin funiculus when fully displayed.

Tree, to 27 m tall and 40 cm dbh, glabrous to puberulent throughout; trunk ± involuted with many prominent horizontal wrinkles; outer bark thin; inner bark reddish; young stems very prominently lenticellate. Petioles margined; rachis margined to narrowly winged; leaflets in 2-5 (usually 4) pairs, narrowly ovate to lanceolate-elliptic or oblanceolate, acuminate, rounded to acute at base, slightly asymmetrical, the terminal pair 8-22 cm long, 2.5-8 cm wide. Spikes axillary in groups of 1-6; peduncles 1.5-3.5 cm long; rachis shorter than peduncle, very densely flowered, 0.5-3 cm long; bracts ca 5 mm long; flowers sessile; calyx 1-2(3) mm long, the lobes ca 0.5 mm long, blunt; corolla 4-8 mm long, the lobes blunt to acute, ca 1 mm long; stamens and style ca 1 cm long. Legumes flat, 10-22 cm long, (2)2.5-3 cm wide, ± glabrous, ± straight, the marginal ribs prominent, the fruits probably mature from July to October. Known only from Panama, from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Bocas del Toro, San Bias, Veraguas, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Colon, Chiriqui, Code, and Panama.

Tree, to 27 m tall and 40 cm dbh, glabrous to puberulent throughout; trunk ± involuted with many prominent horizontal wrinkles; outer bark thin; inner bark reddish; young stems very prominently lenticellate. Petioles margined; rachis margined to narrowly winged; leaflets in 2-5 (usually 4) pairs, narrowly ovate to lanceolate-elliptic or oblanceolate, acuminate, rounded to acute at base, slightly asymmetrical, the terminal pair 8-22 cm long, 2.5-8 cm wide. Spikes axillary in groups of 1-6; peduncles 1.5-3.5 cm long; rachis shorter than peduncle, very densely flowered, 0.5-3 cm long; bracts ca 5 mm long; flowers sessile; calyx 1-2(3) mm long, the lobes ca 0.5 mm long, blunt; corolla 4-8 mm long, the lobes blunt to acute, ca 1 mm long; stamens and style ca 1 cm long. Legumes flat, 10-22 cm long, (2)2.5-3 cm wide, ± glabrous, ± straight, the marginal ribs prominent.

Tree, to 15 m tall; branchlets sparsely strigose when young, glabrate in age, minutely lenticellate, minutely ribbed below petioles (at least when dried). Leaves strigose throughout, especially on axis and midrib of leaflets; petiole and rachis terete to narrowly margined; leaflets in 2 or 3 pairs, lanceolate to elliptic, long-acuminate, acute to rounded at base, the terminal pair 9-18 cm long, 3.5-7.5 cm wide. Spikes axillary, in groups of 1-7; peduncle and rachis strigose; peduncles 2-4 cm long; rachis much shorter, 1-2.5 cm long; bracts subulate, to ± 2 mm long; calyx puberulent, 3-5 mm long, the lobes ± 1 mm long; corolla moderately sericeous, 5-9 mm long, the lobes to 2 mm long; stamens and style to ca 2 cm long. Legumes flat, to 16 cm long and 2 cm wide, minutely puberulent, the margins raised. Common in the forest. Flowers throughout the rainy season (May to December, rarely to January). One individual Inga punctata on Barro Colorado Island flowered for a week in early June in two consecutive years. Mature fruits seen in late dry season. Fruits are similar to those of Inga pezizifera, but that species lacks persistent warty fruit bases. Mexico to Peru; West Indies. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Bocas del Toro, San Bias, Veraguas, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Colon, Chiriqui, Code, and Panama, from tropical wet forest in Panama and Darien and from lower montane wet forest in Chiriqui.

Tree, to 15 m tall; branchlets ferruginous-puberulent when young, glabrous and prominently lenticellate in age. Petioles ribbed, 2-7 cm long; rachis winged; petiole and rachis sparsely ferruginous-pubescent; leaflets in 2-5 pairs, obovate to elliptic, acute to acuminate, obtuse to rounded at base, densely tomentose to puberulent especially on midrib and veins below, the terminal pair 11-26 cm long, 4.5-12 cm wide. Spikes usually axillary in groups of 1-3; peduncles usually sparsely tomentose, 1-5(6) cm long; floral rachis much shorter, 0.5-2(3) cm long; bracts to 12 mm long; calyx and corolla sparsely sericeous; calyx 6-13 (17) mm long, the lobes to 2 mm long; corolla 18-30 mm long, the lobes to 3 mm long; stamens and styles 4-5.5 cm long. Legumes tetragonal with prominently ribbed corners, 11-30 cm long, 1.5-3.5 cm wide, ca 1.5 cm thick, glabrate to densely pubescent. Common, at least along the shore. Seasonal behavior uncertain. Flowers from August to May, especially from November to February. Most fruits mature in the rainy season. An extremely variable species. Often planted for shade in coffee plantations. Mexico to Panama; West Indies. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Bocas del Toro, San Bias, Code, Panama, and Darien and from premontane wet forest in Chiriqui (San Felix).

Tree, 4.5-35 m, the young twigs minutely adpressed-pubescent to glabrescent. Leaves with the petiole 0.5-1.2 cm; blade 10-30 X 3.5-12 cm, elliptical to oblong-elliptical, acute to obtuse or (rarely) subtruncate at the base, glabrous on the underside, without domatia or (rarely) with countable trichomes in the axils of the main veins, with (4)5-8 secondary veins on each side. Inflorescences [of Nectandra purpurea] 10-17 cm. Flowers with the tepals (1—)1.2—2(—2.4) mm. Fruits 1-1.5 cm, ellipsoidal; cup ca. 0.3 cm. Very wet and pluvial forest, 0-1550 m; Caribbean [vertical] Cords. of Guanacaste, Triarán and Central (E.B. La Selva), San Carlos and Tortuguero Plains, Low Talamanca, both [vertical] Cord. de Talamanca, [Pacific] vertical, S Coastal Range (Fila Cruces). Flowers [of Nectandra purpurea] May-Sept.
